newsitem.title: UK: UK Treasury revises upward baseline PSBR.
newsitem.headline: UK Treasury revises upward baseline PSBR.

text.p: The British Treasury said it had adopted new cautious assumptions about the public finances which would have resulted in higher forecasts for the PSBR had they been in place at the time of the last budget in November 1996.

Stressing that is was revising upwards the baseline PSBR and not making new forecasts, the Treasury said the new assumptions would have led to the PSBR being 500 million stg higher in 1997/98 and 3.25 billion stg higher in 1998/99.
The PSBR for 1999/2000 would have been 4.0 billion stg higher, 2000/2001 5-1/2 billion stg higher and 2001/02 7.0 billion stg higher.

The Treasury's assumptions were as follows: - credit will only be taken for privatisation proceeds from sales that have already been announced; - the estimate of savings generated by the "spend to save" programme announced in the November 1996 budget will be limited to the direct effects of the measures and will exclude indirect impacts. The savings are now estimated at 4.9 billion stg compared with the original forecast of 6.7 billion stg; - the assumed underlying rate of the growth in the economy will be 2-1/4 percent per year; - a flat planning assumption for unemployment will be used rather than forecasts of actual unemployment; - assumptions for the level of interest rates will be derived from expectations in financial markets. In the past, Treasury practice was to estimate a path for interest rates necessary to meet the government's inflation target.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown welcomed an independent report into the assumptions underlying the public finances from Sir John Bourn, Comptroller and Auditor General of the National Audit Office, in which the Treasury's new assumptions were published.
"I am delighted that the National Audit Office have provided independent backing for my new assumptions for forecasting public finances," Brown said in a statement.

This was the first time the Treasury's forecasting assumptions had been opened to independent scrutiny. "It means that the budget arithmetic will be based on financial conventions which are open, transparent and accountable," Brown said.
He added that there should be a continuing role for the National Audit Office in subsequent budgets.

The Treasury statement said revised forecasts of the PSBR and other fiscal aggregates would be published on Budget Day on July 2, incorporating the effects of budget measures and the changes in assumptions it had outlined.

Commenting on the Treasury's assumptions, Sir John Bourn said; "While the assumptions adopted by the Chancellor are not the only ones which could be reconciled with the evidence, in my opinion they have been arrived at systematically on the basis of the available data and by methods which interpret it in a reasonable way."
